The child knows a plant is alive even though it does not walk, and does not say plants make no waste or never respond. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Thinks plants are not alive because they do not walk or move about.

example.question: Why do we say a maize plant is a living thing?
example.wrong_answer: It moves from place to place
example.correct_answer: It grows, makes seeds, and responds to its surroundings

misconceptions.cause: The child links being alive with moving the whole body.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It moves from place to place" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Plant a bean seed in a cup and look at it every day: it grows and bends to the window without walking.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants are alive even though they do not walk. They grow, make seeds, remove waste, respond to their surroundings and die.
misconceptions.source: Children's science research reports this idea. Cited from memory: verify the reference.

misconceptions.error: Thinks plants make no waste, only animals do.

example.question: Which of these do living things do? Does a plant remove waste?
example.correct_answer: Yes, plants also get rid of waste

misconceptions.cause: The child links waste with toilets and droppings.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only animals remove waste" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say that plants lose water vapour and gases through their leaves and drop old leaves and fruits.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants also remove waste. They give out waste gases and water through the leaves, and old leaves fall.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks plants do not respond to changes around them.

example.question: A seedling on a window sill bends towards the light. What does this show?
example.wrong_answer: The plant is not alive, it is only leaning
example.correct_answer: The plant responds to light

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks only animals react to things.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The plant is not alive, it is only leaning" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Turn the cup around and watch the seedling bend back over two days.
misconceptions.feedback: Plants respond to their surroundings. A seedling grows towards the light, and the touch-me-not folds its leaves when touched.
misconceptions.source: Children's science research reports this idea. Cited from memory: verify the reference.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the leaves take in water from the soil, or that roots make the plant's food.

example.question: Which part of a plant takes in water from the soil?
example.correct_answer: The roots

misconceptions.cause: The child mixes up where water enters and where food is made.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The leaves" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Put a bean plant in coloured water and see which part first turns colour.
misconceptions.feedback: The roots take in water and mineral salts from the soil. The leaves make food using sunlight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the stem only holds the plant up.

example.question: What does the stem do for a plant?
example.wrong_answer: It only holds the plant up
example.correct_answer: It holds the plant up and carries water and food

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the stem's shape and strength.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It only holds the plant up" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Stand a stem of a white flower in coloured water and see the colour climb up the stem.
misconceptions.feedback: The stem holds the plant up and also carries water and food to the other parts.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks leaves are only for shade or to look green, not to make food.

example.question: What do the leaves of a maize plant do?
example.correct_answer: They make food for the plant using sunlight

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen leaves as decoration or shelter.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They give shade only" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Cover one leaf with dark paper for a week and look at how it fades.
misconceptions.feedback: Leaves are the kitchen of the plant. They make food using sunlight.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks animals reproduce only by giving birth to live young (not by eggs).

example.question: How do birds and fish reproduce?
example.wrong_answer: They give birth to live young like a cow
example.correct_answer: They lay eggs

misconceptions.cause: The child has met the cow and the goat at home and not the egg.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "They give birth to live young like a cow" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List animals that lay eggs (hen, fish, frog, snake) and animals that give birth (cow, goat, dog).
misconceptions.feedback: Reproducing is making new animals. Some give birth to live young. Birds, fish, frogs and snakes lay eggs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an animal that lies still or sleeps is not alive.

example.question: A lizard lies still in the sun. Is it alive?
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is only resting and is still breathing

misconceptions.cause: The child links being alive with moving all the time.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, it is not moving" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Watch a sleeping cat: its sides move as it breathes.
misconceptions.feedback: An animal that is resting or asleep is still alive. It still breathes and feeds when it wakes.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks insects, worms and fish are not animals (only cows, goats, lions and other big animals are).

example.question: Is a butterfly an animal?
example.wrong_answer: No, only big animals are animals
example.correct_answer: Yes, it is an animal

misconceptions.cause: The child uses "animal" to mean the big mammals.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "No, only big animals are animals" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List every living thing in the school compound that is not a plant: ants, birds, worms are animals too.
misconceptions.feedback: Insects, worms, fish and birds are all animals. An animal is a living thing that feeds and moves and is not a plant.
misconceptions.source: Children's science research reports this idea. Cited from memory: verify the reference.

misconceptions.error: Thinks an animal with no legs (snake, fish) has no backbone.

example.question: Is a snake a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: An invertebrate, it has no legs
example.correct_answer: A vertebrate, it has a backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child looks at legs and not at the backbone.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "An invertebrate, it has no legs" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Feel your own backbone, then show a picture of a snake skeleton with its many small bones in a line.
misconceptions.feedback: A snake has a backbone, with many small bones in a row. So a snake is a vertebrate even without legs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks every animal with legs is a vertebrate (spider, ant, grasshopper, crab).

example.question: Is a grasshopper a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
example.correct_answer: An invertebrate, it has no backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child links legs with bones.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A vertebrate, it has legs" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look at a dead grasshopper: legs, but the body is soft inside a hard cover and there is no backbone.
misconceptions.feedback: A grasshopper has six legs but no backbone, so it is an invertebrate. Legs do not make a vertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a hard shell or hard cover (snail, crab, beetle) is a backbone.

example.question: Is a snail a vertebrate or an invertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: A vertebrate, it has a hard shell
example.correct_answer: An invertebrate, the shell is not a backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child treats anything hard as bone.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A vertebrate, it has a hard shell" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Note that a shell is on the outside and a backbone is inside the body along the back.
misconceptions.feedback: A snail's shell is a hard cover on the outside. A backbone is inside the body. The snail has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks small animals are invertebrates and big ones are vertebrates (a chick, a mouse or a small frog taken as invertebrates).

example.question: Why is a small frog a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: It is not, because it is small
example.correct_answer: It has a backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child uses size as the rule.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It is not, because it is small" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare a large earthworm and a tiny chick: the small chick has a backbone and the long worm has none.
misconceptions.feedback: Size does not matter. A tiny frog or a chick has a backbone, so it is a vertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Uses wings or the number of legs as the rule for vertebrates.

example.question: Which rule tells us an animal is an invertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: It has more than four legs
example.correct_answer: It has no backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child picks a visible feature that is not the rule.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It has more than four legs" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Sort pictures only by the backbone and ignore legs, wings and size.
misconceptions.feedback: The only rule is the backbone. An animal with no backbone is an invertebrate, whatever its legs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks all animals that live in water are vertebrates, or that all animals on land are.

example.question: Is a crab, which lives in water, a vertebrate?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, because it lives in water like fish
example.correct_answer: No, it has no backbone

misconceptions.cause: The child sorts by where animals live.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, because it lives in water like fish" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Find crabs, snails and jellyfish among water animals that are invertebrates.
misconceptions.feedback: Where an animal lives does not decide it. A crab lives in water but has no backbone, so it is an invertebrate.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

sub_strands.authoring_notes: Outcome c (appreciate the need to care for animals) is attitudinal: observe it in care of a class pet or school animals. Outcomes a and b are tested by questions; classifying living animals from a nature walk is better checked by the teacher.

skills.name: Name the parts of the human digestive system and say what each does
skills.mastery: The child names the mouth (teeth chew food), the oesophagus or food pipe (carries food to the stomach), the stomach (churns food into a soft mixture), the small intestine (digested food goes into the blood), the large intestine (takes in water, leaving waste) and the anus (waste leaves). The child does not mix up the food pipe and the windpipe or say the stomach does all the work. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

skills.name: Put the parts of the digestive system in the order food passes through them
skills.mastery: The child gives the path of food as mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus. The child does not put the large intestine before the small intestine and does not think the small intestine is the short one. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

skills.name: Choose habits that keep the digestive system healthy
skills.mastery: The child chooses habits that protect the digestive system: wash hands with soap before eating and after the toilet, drink clean boiled or treated water, eat a balanced diet with fruits, vegetables and fibre, chew food well, and keep food covered. The child knows that sweets or soda do not replace water or meals, and that washing food alone is not enough. Writing a whole plan is a task for the teacher to mark: this skill is the knowledge for it. Evidence rule: at least four of the last five fresh questions right across at least two question forms, and no repeated pick of the same misconception.

misconceptions.error: Mixes up the food pipe (oesophagus) with the windpipe.

example.question: Which tube carries food from the mouth to the stomach?
example.correct_answer: The oesophagus (food pipe)

misconceptions.cause: The child links "pipe in the neck" with food and air together.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The windpipe" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say the food pipe is for food and the windpipe is for air to the lungs.
misconceptions.feedback: The oesophagus, also called the food pipe, carries food to the stomach. The windpipe carries air to the lungs.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the stomach does all the digesting and takes in all the food.

example.question: Where does most digested food go into the blood?
example.correct_answer: The small intestine

misconceptions.cause: The child knows the stomach is the "food bag" and nothing more.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The stomach" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say the stomach churns the food and the small intestine takes the good parts into the blood.
misconceptions.feedback: The stomach churns food into a soft mixture. Most digested food goes into the blood in the small intestine.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the large intestine takes in food (rather than water) or makes the food.

example.question: What does the large intestine take in from the leftover food?
example.correct_answer: Water

misconceptions.cause: The child expects the biggest tube to do the biggest job on food.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Most of the food" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say that the small intestine takes the food and the large intestine takes water and leaves the waste.
misconceptions.feedback: The large intestine takes in water from the leftover food. What is left is waste that leaves through the anus.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Puts the large intestine before the small intestine.

example.question: Which comes first after the stomach?
example.correct_answer: The small intestine

misconceptions.cause: The child follows the words large then small.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The large intestine" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Trace the path with a finger on a body chart: stomach, long small intestine, then large intestine.
misconceptions.feedback: After the stomach, food goes to the small intestine, and then to the large intestine.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks the small intestine is short (small in length).

example.question: Which part of the intestine is longer?
example.correct_answer: The small intestine is longer (it is narrow, not short)

misconceptions.cause: The child hears small as short.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The small intestine is short" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Measure a long string and say it stands for the small intestine, about six metres in an adult. The large intestine is wider and about 1.5 metres.
misconceptions.feedback: The small intestine is narrow but very long. The large intestine is wider but shorter.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks food goes straight from the mouth to the stomach (leaves out the oesophagus), or that the stomach is the last part.

example.question: Which part is the last in the path of food?
example.correct_answer: The anus

misconceptions.cause: The child stops the path at the stomach, where the food seems to go.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The stomach" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Count the six parts with a finger, mouth to anus.
misconceptions.feedback: Food passes through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine and anus. The anus is last.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks washing food is enough, so washing hands does not matter.

example.question: Wanjiru washes the mangoes but not her hands. Is this enough?
example.wrong_answer: Yes, clean food is all that matters
example.correct_answer: No, she should wash her hands with soap too

misconceptions.cause: The child sees only the food as a source of germs.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yes, clean food is all that matters" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Look at dirty hands under a lens and then at clean ones.
misconceptions.feedback: Hands carry germs to the mouth. Wash the food and wash your hands with soap before you eat.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks soda or sweets can take the place of water and meals.

example.question: What should Baraka drink most of through the day?
example.correct_answer: Clean water

misconceptions.cause: The child has seen drinks as the same as water.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Soda" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Compare how much sugar sits in a bottle of soda with a glass of water.
misconceptions.feedback: Clean water keeps the digestive system working. Soda and sweets are not a replacement for water or a balanced meal.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks any clear water from a stream is safe to drink without boiling or treating.

example.question: Njeri finds clear water in a stream. What should she do before drinking it?
example.correct_answer: Boil it or treat it first

misconceptions.error: Thinks the only use of heat is to cook.

example.question: Which of these is also a use of heat?
example.wrong_answer: There is no other use, only cooking
example.correct_answer: Drying grain and warming a house

misconceptions.cause: The child links heat with the kitchen.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "There is no other use, only cooking" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: List five jobs done with heat at home and on the farm.
misconceptions.feedback: Heat is used for cooking and also for drying, warming, ironing and boiling water.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks butter, oil or ash should be put on a burn.

example.question: A child burns her hand. What should be done first?
example.correct_answer: Put the burn under cool running water

misconceptions.cause: This is a common home custom.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Rub butter on it" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say that cool water takes the heat out of the skin.
misconceptions.feedback: Put a burn under cool running water for several minutes. Do not put butter, oil or ash on it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a lit stove or jiko can be refilled with paraffin or charcoal while burning.

example.question: A paraffin stove is nearly empty and still burning. What is the safe thing to do?
example.wrong_answer: Pour more paraffin in at once
example.correct_answer: Put it out, let it cool, then refill

misconceptions.cause: The child wants to save time.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Pour more paraffin in at once" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say that paraffin catches fire from a flame.
misconceptions.feedback: Put out the flame, let the stove cool, and then refill it.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a wet cloth is good for holding a hot pot.

example.question: What should you use to lift a hot pot?
example.correct_answer: A dry cloth or pot holder

misconceptions.cause: The child thinks wet cools the pot.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A wet cloth" next to the right answer and ask the question again in a new context.
misconceptions.help: Say that steam from a wet cloth burns.
misconceptions.feedback: Use a dry cloth or pot holder. A wet cloth lets the heat through and the steam can burn.
misconceptions.source: To confirm by a teacher: a common classroom error, not traced to a study by the author.
